title: The Zohar
hookLine: in Castile, Moses de León circulates the Zohar, the book of radiance

cards: In a town in Castile, a scholar named Moses de León starts sending out pages: copies, he says, of an old book.
It's written mostly in Aramaic, a language of the Talmud, and it reads like a long walk through the Torah with a circle of ancient teachers, led by a rabbi of the Mishnah, Shimon bar Yochai.
They stop on a verse, one of them opens it, and the verse turns out to have rooms inside rooms. Scholars, students and mystics begin copying the pages. The book has a one-word name: Zohar.

teach.b: The name comes from a verse in the book of Daniel.

teach.h: SHALL SHINE AS THE BRIGHTNESS OF THE FIRMAMENT.
teach.b: In the JPS translation: "And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament." Brightness there is zohar. So the title means radiance, splendor, a light that shines, and the book is about hidden light.
The Zohar reads the Torah as having a surface and a depth: the stories and laws are the garment; underneath is a soul.
It speaks of the sefirot, ways that the hidden God is revealed in the world, and it imagines human actions, a prayer, a kind deed, a Sabbath meal, echoing up through those worlds.

Now the honest part: who wrote it? There are two answers, both held sincerely. Traditional readers receive the Zohar as the teaching of Shimon bar Yochai and his companions, handed down and later brought to light.
Other readers, historians among them, look at its language and its world and conclude it was composed in Castile in the time of Moses de León, by him or a circle around him.
There's even an old account of a traveler, Isaac of Acre, who went looking for the ancient original and heard conflicting answers. Both views agree on what happened next.
The Zohar became a central book of Kabbalah, Jewish mystical teaching. Its ideas flowed into prayer books, Sabbath songs and later movements of the spirit.
People still sit with it slowly, a line at a time, the way its own teachers sit with a verse.

how: Some Jews study the Zohar in groups or read a portion daily, and its teachings shaped customs like the Friday night Kabbalat Shabbat service and some Sabbath songs.

games.q: you are Isaac of Acre, a traveler who has heard of an ancient book appearing in Castile. what do you do?
o: copy it and ask no questions.
go to Castile and look for the ancient original.
refuse to read it at all.
games.why: an old account says he went looking for the original manuscript and heard conflicting answers. the question of authorship is still discussed.

practice: Take the verse the book is named for, and they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, breathing in on the first half and out on the second.
Then ask the Zohar's kind of question, what makes a person shine, and let the line sit without solving it. If you pray, you can carry the verse into your own prayer.

wordCard.voice: Zohar. Brightness, radiance, from a verse in Daniel: the name of a central book of Jewish mysticism, written mostly in Aramaic and circulated from Castile. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: brightness, radiance, as in Daniel's 'brightness of the firmament'.
